alternative: Explicit setter functions that return a status code, checked between calls, or - for configuration - a plain struct filled with C99 designated initializers (`.width = 640`) and passed to one constructor; keep chaining only for infallible helpers with no error channel to lose.
idiom_name: free functions returning the receiver: widget_t *widget_set_title(widget_t *w, const char *t)
implementation_notes: C has no methods, no receiver and no overloading, so the classic chain collapses into free functions whose first parameter is the object and whose return value is that same pointer (widget_set_width(w, 640) returning w). It compiles and a few libraries are shaped this way, but the style fights C's error model - a function that must hand the object back cannot also return a status code - and C's diagnostics, because the chain is one expression with no intermediate variables to inspect. What replaces the structure: a configuration struct filled with C99 designated initializers, which names each setting at the call site while members that are not mentioned are zero-initialized, or a run of statements that checks each status before the next call. Keep a chain only for steps that cannot fail and for allocation-free helpers that already return the destination (the strcat/strcpy convention of returning dest).
pitfalls: A step that can fail forces the chain to swallow its status: `w = widget_set_title(w, "x")` compiles even when the call failed and left w untouched, so the failure surfaces arbitrarily later.
Chaining through function-pointer tables (w->ops->set_title(w, ...)) needs a second receiver convention and makes the printed call site heavier, not lighter - the usual C attempt at method chaining.
A chain that allocates its receiver inside the expression (widget_new()->set_width(...)) leaks or dangles unless ownership is documented per step; C gives no destructor to rely on.
